lines.speaker: Zenophantus
lines.text: So, Callidemides, how did you die? I choked to death on too much food as Deinius's parasite, as you know—you were there when it happened.

lines.speaker: Callidemides
lines.text: I was there, Zenophantus. But my case turned out to be something of a paradox. You know old Ptoiodorus, I suppose?

lines.speaker: Zenophantus
lines.text: The childless rich man? I knew you spent most of your time with him.

lines.speaker: Callidemides
lines.text: I danced attendance on him constantly, with him promising all along to die in my favor. But the whole business dragged on forever and the old man lived longer than Tithonus, so I found a shortcut to the inheritance. I bought some poison and persuaded the cupbearer: whenever Ptoiodorus asked for a drink—and he drinks it pretty strong—to have it mixed in a cup ready and serve it to him. If he did that, I swore I'd set him free.

lines.speaker: Zenophantus
lines.text: What happened then? You look like you're about to tell something ridiculous.

lines.speaker: Callidemides
lines.text: We'd just come back from the baths. The young fellow had two cups ready—one with the poison for Ptoiodorus, the other plain for me. Somehow or other he slipped up and gave me the poison and the safe one to Ptoiodorus. So the old man drank, and I dropped dead on the spot, the substitute corpse instead of him. Why are you laughing at this, Zenophantus? You shouldn't laugh at a friend.

lines.speaker: Zenophantus
lines.text: [laughs] That's a neat twist, Callidemides. What did the old man do about it?

lines.speaker: Callidemides
lines.text: He was startled at first by the suddenness, then realized what had happened and laughed himself, at what the cupbearer had managed.

lines.speaker: Zenophantus
lines.text: Still, you shouldn't have taken the shortcut. It would have reached you more safely by the main road, even if a bit slower.
